opus-5.5.text:
I think one thing that's still underappreciated is how much progress is coming from the systems and efficiency side rather than just from scaling up. People tend to focus on the headline model releases, but a lot of what makes those models usable — longer context, cheaper inference, faster training — comes from work on things like better attention kernels, quantization, and making sure we're actually using the hardware well. When you can make inference two or three times cheaper, that changes what applications are economically viable, and I don't think that gets as much attention as a new benchmark number does.

Related to that, I'd point to architecture research beyond the standard Transformer. There's been a lot of interesting work on state space models, linear attention variants, and hybrid architectures that mix a few attention layers with these more efficient layers. For a while people assumed the Transformer was the final answer, but especially as we move toward workloads like long-context reasoning, agents that run for a long time, and processing video or audio, the cost of attention scaling quadratically really starts to bite. Hybrid models seem to get you most of the quality with much better throughput, and I think we'll see more of that in production.

And the last thing I'd mention is inference-time compute. Now that models are doing a lot more reasoning at test time, generating long chains of thought, the bottleneck shifts from training to inference. That makes efficiency research even more important, because every improvement in decoding speed translates directly into either lower cost or more thinking the model can do for the same budget. So I'd say the intersection of algorithms, architecture, and hardware is where a lot of the real leverage is, and it deserves more attention than it gets.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the thing that gets underappreciated is just how much of the progress in AI right now is really about systems and hardware co-design, not just new model ideas. Everyone talks about architectures and scaling laws, but a huge fraction of the gains over the past few years have come from squeezing more out of the hardware we already have: better memory management, better kernels, better ways to map the computation onto the GPU's memory hierarchy.

FlashAttention is the example I know best, obviously. The attention algorithm didn't change. What changed was recognizing that the bottleneck was memory bandwidth rather than compute, and restructuring the computation so you never materialize the big attention matrix in slow memory. That one observation made long context practical. And I'd argue there are many more of those opportunities sitting around, because the hardware keeps changing faster than the software stack adapts. Every new generation of accelerator has different ratios of compute to bandwidth, new tensor core shapes, new ways to move data, and it takes a year or two for the algorithms to catch up.

The second thing I'd point to is the renewed interest in alternatives to standard attention. State space models, linear attention, hybrid architectures that mix a few attention layers with recurrent-style layers. For a while the field assumed the transformer was the end of history. I don't think that's right. The transformer is wonderful because it's so hardware-friendly, but the quadratic cost in sequence length is real, and inference cost is becoming the dominant concern as models get deployed at scale. Architectures with constant-size state per token change the economics of serving. Even if they're not strictly better in quality, a hybrid that's two or three times cheaper to run at long context is a very big deal commercially, and that hasn't fully sunk in.

And the third one, which is related: inference efficiency generally. Training gets the headlines because that's where the giant clusters are, but most of the FLOPs in the world are going to be spent on inference, and inference is a totally different regime. It's memory-bound, it's latency-sensitive, you're doing batched decoding with tiny matrix multiplies. Things like speculative decoding, better KV cache management, quantization that actually preserves quality, these are quiet improvements that compound. If you can serve the same model at a third of the cost, that's equivalent to a pretty significant capability jump from the user's point of view, because you can afford to run a bigger model or think longer per query.

So if I had to summarize: pay attention to the boring layer. The kernels, the memory hierarchy, the serving stack. That's where a lot of the real leverage is right now.

astra-6.text:
I think the efficiency side of AI deserves more attention. People tend to focus on model size and benchmark results, but how efficiently we train and run these models determines who can experiment with them and what applications are practical.

One thing I find particularly interesting is the interaction between algorithms and hardware. You can have two algorithms that do roughly the same amount of arithmetic, but one runs much faster because it moves less data between different levels of memory. So counting operations alone doesn’t tell you how fast something will be.

That creates a lot of opportunities. Better attention implementations, better ways to use lower precision, and architectures designed with hardware in mind can make experimentation much cheaper. And when more people can try ideas and iterate quickly, that can change the pace of research.

sol-6.1.text:
One direction I think deserves more attention is making better use of the compute we already have. We talk a lot about larger models and more GPUs, but there’s still a lot of room to improve how efficiently we train models and run inference.

With FlashAttention, for example, the key insight was that moving data between different parts of GPU memory can be more expensive than doing the actual arithmetic. So you can compute the same attention operation much faster by changing how you organize the computation.

I’m also excited about architectures beyond Transformers, particularly state space models. Attention is powerful, but it’s worth asking whether every part of a model needs it. Can we combine attention with other ways of processing sequences to get strong performance with lower memory usage and faster generation? That interaction between algorithms and hardware is where I think a lot of interesting progress can happen.
